lines: Bin dokuz yüz yirmi dokuz. İstanbul, Topkapı Sarayı.
Saray müzeye dönüşürken, kütüphanede katlanmış bir deri bulunur.
Üzerinde, dört yüz yıllık bir dünya haritası vardır.
Dört yüz on altı yıl önce, Gelibolu'da bir denizci kalemi eline alır.
Adı Piri Reis. Amcası, ünlü kaptan Kemal Reis.
Haritayı bin beş yüz on üç yılında, ceylan derisine çizer.
Kenarına, yaklaşık yirmi eski haritayı birleştirdiğini yazar.
Bunlardan biri, bugün kayıp olan bir Kolomb haritasıdır.
Haritada İspanya, Afrika kıyısı ve Güney Amerika görünür.
Sekiz yıl sonra denizciler için bir kitap yazar: Kitab-ı Bahriye.
Akdeniz'in koyları ve limanları, tek tek çizilidir.
Bugün haritanın yalnızca üçte biri elimizde.
Ve o deri, hâlâ Topkapı Sarayı'nda saklanıyor.

acts.why: 1929 is the newsreel era: the discovery is told like a period news film
back to 1513: the world of printed charts, sepia and engraved type
the lost Columbus map turns it into an investigation: dossier print, stamps, highlights
back to the present the film opened in: the same newsreel closes the circle

ideas: The Imperial Gate of Topkapı Palace in a flickering newsreel frame, the date 1929 stamped above the crowd
Library shelves of Ottoman manuscripts inside the palace, where a folded skin waits between the books
The Piri Reis map itself fills the frame, then the camera dives to its painted ships and compass rose
A timeline jumps back from 1929 to 1513 and lands on Gelibolu, where a sailor picks up his pen
Kemal Reis's flagship Göke in an Ottoman miniature, the ship the young Piri sailed under his uncle
A route draws across the Mediterranean from Gelibolu past Rhodes and Crete to the Strait of Gibraltar
The year 1513 counts up over the cracked gazelle-skin texture of the original chart
Two older charts of the kind he names as sources fan onto the desk: al-Idrisi's world map and the Portuguese Cantino planisphere
A portrait of Christopher Columbus receives a red LOST stamp, because his map that Piri copied is gone
Spain, the African coast and the bulge of South America light up one by one on a map of the Atlantic
A page of the Kitab-ı Bahriye with a harbour chart, a highlight sweeping across its handwritten title
The camera follows a coastline drawn in the book, every bay and harbour named in red ink
Only the left third of the world map survives: the surviving fragment lights up, the missing two thirds stay grey
The torn right edge of the parchment where the rest of the world once continued, in a slow push
The palace on the Bosphorus at dusk: the skin is still kept here, almost a century after it was found
